title: Efficient black-box testing of high-dimensional convexity
formal: For each fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), is there a randomized adaptive membership-query tester that, for every dimension \(n\) and every Borel set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), distinguishes convexity from Gaussian distance at least \(\varepsilon\) to every convex set using at most \(C_\varepsilon n^{c_\varepsilon}\) queries and with error probability at most \(1/3\) on each promised input? This is ordinary two-sided testing, not tolerant testing.
definitions:
The standard Gaussian measure \(\gamma_n\) has density \((2\pi)^{-n/2}\exp(-\|x\|_2^2/2)\) on \(\mathbb R^n\). A set \(K\) is convex if \((1-t)x+ty\in K\) for every \(x,y\in K\) and \(t\in[0,1]\). Its distance from \(S\) is the Gaussian measure of the symmetric difference, \(\gamma_n(S\triangle K)\). Define distance to convexity as the infimum of this quantity over Borel convex sets \(K\), including the empty set and all of \(\mathbb R^n\).

An oracle returns the exact bit \(1_S(x)\) for a requested point \(x\). Queries can be chosen adaptively. The query model is an information model over exact real points: a randomized decision tree may choose points by measurable functions of its internal randomness and previous answer bits, with arbitrary measurable computation free. Independent Gaussian random points can be generated internally, but obtaining their membership labels costs queries. There is no oracle supplying samples conditioned on membership in \(S\), a boundary, a separation hyperplane or a finite description of the set.

The tester must accept every convex input with probability at least \(2/3\), and reject every input whose distance to convexity is at least \(\varepsilon\) with probability at least \(2/3\). Either output is allowed in the gap. Success probability is over its internal randomness on each fixed oracle, and the query bound is worst-case over oracles and random choices. Both false acceptance and false rejection are permitted. Constants and the polynomial degree may depend on the fixed accuracy but not on dimension or the set. This is an oracle-query claim, not a polynomial bound on finite-precision arithmetic or point representation.

Restricting to Borel inputs makes all measures and probabilities defined; the source's arbitrary measurable-set formulation is interpreted with this regularity convention. A tolerant tester would also have to accept nonconvex sets close to convexity. That additional promise is not required here.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked affirmative proof of a family of testers with the stated polynomial query bounds for every fixed accuracy, or a complete Lean-checked refutation. A refutation must exclude adaptive two-sided testers, not only one-sided or nonadaptive procedures. A sample-only lower bound or a tolerant-testing lower bound is insufficient. A theorem about query count alone need not prove a comparable bound on all arithmetic operations.
context:
Chen and collaborators study Gaussian convexity testing using a black-box membership oracle. Their primary paper separates ordinary and tolerant testing, and adaptive and nonadaptive access.

The checked results include polynomial lower bounds for one-sided adaptive and two-sided nonadaptive ordinary testing, and a mildly exponential lower bound for nonadaptive tolerant testing. The latter is a stronger acceptance requirement and does not exclude the polynomial-query ordinary tester asked for here.
why: This asks whether a basic high-dimensional geometric property is accessible through a small black-box interface.

import_provenance.original_title: Efficient black-box testing of high-dimensional convexity
import_provenance.original_statement: Given membership-query access to S⊆R^n, can convexity versus constant Gaussian-measure distance from every convex set be tested with poly(n) queries? Chen and coauthors prove polynomial query lower bounds, while the general upper bound is 2^{Õ(√n)} for constant accuracy, leaving the basic polynomial-versus-superpolynomial question open.

The tester must distinguish a convex set from one a fixed Gaussian distance away from every convex set.
The card permits adaptive queries and two-sided error, measuring only the number of membership answers.
Known lower bounds distinguish this model from tolerant or one-sided testing.
The target asks whether convexity can be recognized from polynomially much black-box information.
